\section*{\texorpdfstring{Smooth 4-Dimensional Poincaré Conjecture}{Smooth 4-Dimensional Poincaré Conjecture}}\label{18}

\subsection{Definitions and mathematical statement}
A closed manifold is compact without boundary. A smooth homotopy $4$-sphere is a smooth closed $4$-manifold $M$ for which there exist continuous maps $M\leftrightarrows S^4$ whose compositions are homotopic to the identities. The conjecture is
\[
 M\simeq S^4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad M\cong_{\rm diff} S^4.
\]
A diffeomorphism must be smooth with smooth inverse. A homeomorphism alone does not settle this smooth-category question.
\par\smallskip\textit{Formulation and concept references:} \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.10938}{[S1]}.

\subsection{Short English statement}
Is every smooth four-dimensional space with the homotopy type of a sphere smoothly the standard sphere?

\subsection{Research attempt}
\paragraph{Current frontier.}
\textit{Research check: 27 September 2026.}
Gerig's construction gives a particular ECH/Seiberg--Witten-based invariant
that is constant on homotopy four-spheres; the result is an obstruction to
that invariant, not a classification of smooth structures. His Section 1
also records the extension theorem for diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ and the
Cerf--Palais disk theorem. \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.10938}{[S1]}.
The retrieved research does not supply a verified resolution of the full
smooth problem. The catalogue's code-review link is retained as supplied,
but no formal proof in that repository has been imported or certified in
this attempt. A claim about a formalization would require checking its
actual theorem and dependencies, not its filename.

\paragraph{Attack route.}
An invariant route needs a quantity that is both computable and sensitive
to a possible exotic sphere; a handle route needs geometric cancellation;
and a puncturing route needs control of the smooth end, not just the
homotopy type. We combine the latter two to locate exactly which data an
algebraic cancellation argument discards.

\paragraph{Attempt: the compact puncture criterion.}
Let $M$ be a smooth homotopy four-sphere and remove the interior of a
small smoothly embedded standard ball $B$. The compact manifold
$C=M\setminus\operatorname{int}B$ has boundary $S^3$ and is contractible.
Indeed, van Kampen applied with a collar to $M=C\cup B$ gives
$\pi_1(C)=\pi_1(M)=0$. In Mayer--Vietoris, the boundary map
$H_4(M,{\mathbb{Z}})\to H_3(S^3,{\mathbb{Z}})$ sends the oriented fundamental class to the
boundary fundamental class and is an isomorphism. Exactness, together
with the vanishing of the other reduced homology groups of $M$ and $B$,
then gives $\widetilde H_i(C,{\mathbb{Z}})=0$ for every $i$.
A compact smooth manifold has finite CW type. If any higher homotopy group
of $C$ were nonzero, its first nonzero one would give a nonzero homology
group by Hurewicz; hence all vanish, and Whitehead's theorem gives
contractibility.

If $C$ is diffeomorphic to $D^4$, capping it with $B$ gives two standard
balls glued along an $S^3$ diffeomorphism. After adjusting orientations,
that diffeomorphism extends across a ball by the theorem quoted in
Gerig's Theorem 1.2. The double is therefore standard $S^4$.
Conversely, if $M$ is standard, Cerf--Palais (Gerig's Theorem 1.3) makes
the embedded ball ambiently isotopic to a standard small ball, so its
compact complement is a standard ball. \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.10938}{[S1]}.
Thus the full sphere problem is equivalent to the assertion that every
smooth compact contractible four-manifold with boundary diffeomorphic to
$S^3$ is a standard ball: any such manifold can be capped to give a
homotopy sphere, by the same van Kampen and homology argument.

\paragraph{Attempt: what the handle chain complex really proves.}
Take a handle decomposition of $M$ with one 0-handle and one 4-handle;
write $a,b,c$ for the numbers of 1-, 2-, and 3-handles. The cellular
chain complex has the middle part
\[
 0\longrightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}^c\xrightarrow{\partial_3}{\mathbb{Z}}^b
       \xrightarrow{\partial_2}{\mathbb{Z}}^a\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{22.1}
\]
It is exact: $H_1=H_2=H_3=0$, while the top and bottom differentials
vanish with these oriented single extreme handles. It follows that
$b=a+c$. Since free abelian groups are projective, (22.1) splits. Choose
preimages of a basis of ${\mathbb{Z}}^a$ and a basis of $\ker\partial_2$ given by
$\partial_3$. In these bases the matrices are exactly
\[
 \partial_2=\begin{pmatrix}I_a&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \partial_3=\begin{pmatrix}0\\I_c\end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{22.2}
\]
This establishes algebraic cancellation of the entire middle chain
complex with no assumption on an invariant.

It does not establish geometric handle cancellation. The matrix entries
count signed intersections. The algebraic count $+1$ is compatible with
geometric intersections of signs $+1,+1,-1$; changing bases does not by
itself provide a framed embedded Whitney disk removing the last pair.
Similarly, abelianized attaching words do not determine the fundamental
group or the attaching-link isotopy class. For a concrete warning, consider
\[
 \langle x,y\mid (xy)^2=x^3,\;x^3=y^5\rangle.
 \tag{22.3}
\]
Its exponent-sum matrix is
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&2\\3&-5\end{smallmatrix}\right)$,
with determinant $-1$, yet it has a nontrivial quotient: in $A_5$, choose
$x=(1\,2\,3)$ and $y=(1\,4\,3\,2\,5)$ (composition right to left).
Then $x^3=y^5=1$ and $xy=(1\,4)(2\,5)$, so both relators vanish.
The image is nontrivial. This example is not claimed to present the
fundamental group of a homotopy sphere. It proves only that a unimodular
exponent matrix cannot replace the nonabelian or geometric conditions.

A valid sufficient cancellation statement must instead produce actual
handle slides and isotopies for which each paired attaching sphere meets
its corresponding belt sphere in one transverse point with the required
framing, with a valid successive cancellation order. If all middle
handles cancel in this sense, only a 0- and a 4-handle remain and the
sphere is standard by the extension theorem. The algebra in (22.2)
does not produce those moves.

\paragraph{Stress test.}
Contractibility is a homotopy conclusion, not a diffeomorphism to a ball.
A diffeomorphism of the open puncture to ${\mathbb{R}}^4$ also cannot simply be
assumed to extend over a chosen compactification; Gerig explicitly
separates this end issue. \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.10938}{[S1]}.
Nor can a high-dimensional Whitney or h-cobordism argument be applied
without checking its dimension assumptions. The algebraic cancellation
above is valid in dimension four precisely because it never asserts the
missing embedded-disk move. The finite permutation test for (22.3)
checks the advertised group-theoretic obstruction, not a Kirby diagram.

\paragraph{Outcome.}
\textbf{Outcome: Exploratory approach with unresolved gap.}
The compact-puncture reduction and the exact split chain complex are
established within their stated scope. A unimodular but nontrivial
presentation explicitly breaks the attempt to upgrade homology to
geometric cancellation. No exotic homotopy sphere and no universal
geometric cancellation procedure is supplied. A solution still needs
smooth attaching and end control that survives the loss of information
in the chain complex.

\subsection{Sources}
\begin{itemize}
\item[S1] Chris Gerig, No homotopy 4-sphere invariants using ECH = SWF, Algebraic \& Geometric Topology 21 (2021), Conjecture 1.1.
\url{https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.10938}.
{\small\textit{Catalogue formulation source.}}
\item[S2] smooth4pc-t73-lean: Independent Review.
\url{https://github.com/toffee-desuwa/smooth4pc-t73-lean/blob/main/docs/INDEPENDENT_REVIEW.md}.
{\small\textit{Catalogue research/status reference; not a proof endorsement.}}
\item[S3] The Smooth Four-Dimensional Poincare Conjecture.
\url{https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/smooth-poincare-4d}.
{\small\textit{Catalogue research/status reference; not a proof endorsement.}}
\end{itemize}

\section*{\texorpdfstring{Smooth 4-Dimensional Poincaré Conjecture}{Smooth 4-Dimensional Poincaré Conjecture}}\label{18}

\subsection{Definitions and mathematical statement}
A closed manifold is compact without boundary. A smooth homotopy $4$-sphere is a smooth closed $4$-manifold $M$ for which there exist continuous maps $M\leftrightarrows S^4$ whose compositions are homotopic to the identities. The conjecture is
\[
 M\simeq S^4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad M\cong_{\rm diff} S^4.
\]
A diffeomorphism must be smooth with smooth inverse. A homeomorphism alone does not settle this smooth-category question.
\par\smallskip\textit{Formulation and concept references:} \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.10938}{[S1]}.

\subsection{Short English statement}
Is every smooth four-dimensional space with the homotopy type of a sphere smoothly the standard sphere?

\subsection{Research attempt}
This unresolved attempt by GPT-6 Astra Ultra was prepared on 27 September
2026, using explicit reductions, source checks, and adversarial verification.

\paragraph{Scope, checked inputs, and two routes.}
The target is a diffeomorphism, not a homeomorphism, for every smooth
closed homotopy four-sphere. This attempt pursues a proof route through
geometric handle cancellation and a disproof route through a compact
contractible manifold with boundary $S^3$. It derives precise sufficient
certificates for each route and tests what information would be lost by
replacing geometry with matrices or a finite group computation.

Gerig \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.10938}{[S1]}, Theorems 1.2 and 1.3, records two inputs used below: an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $S^3$ extends across $D^4$
(Cerf), and equi-oriented embedded closed four-balls in a connected
four-manifold are ambient isotopic (Cerf--Palais). His invariant result
is not a classification of all smooth homotopy spheres. The source
repository \href{https://github.com/toffee-desuwa/smooth4pc-t73-lean/blob/main/docs/INDEPENDENT_REVIEW.md}{[S2]}, under its review boundary, explicitly leaves geometric
interfaces as hypotheses of its formalized implication. No external Lean
code was executed and no counterexample is accepted here on that basis.

The handle and knot strategies have substantial precedents, notably
Freedman--Gompf--Morrison--Walker \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.5177}{[E1]}. What follows is a written derivation
and adversarial check of these routes, without a novelty claim.

\paragraph{Lemma 22.1: an equivalent compact-boundary problem.}
The smooth four-dimensional Poincar\'e conjecture is equivalent to:
every smooth compact contractible four-manifold $W$ with
$\partial W\cong S^3$ is diffeomorphic to $D^4$.

\emph{Proof.} First let $M$ be a homotopy four-sphere, choose a smooth
embedded closed ball $B$, and put $W=M\setminus\operatorname{int}B$.
Van Kampen, applied using boundary collars, gives
$\pi_1(M)\cong\pi_1(W)$ because $B$ and $S^3$ are simply connected.
Thus $W$ is simply connected. Excision identifies
$H_*(M,W;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_*(D^4,S^3;\mathbb Z)$. In the long exact
sequence, the map $H_4(M)\to H_4(M,W)$ is an isomorphism: it sends the
oriented fundamental class to the local relative fundamental class.
Together with the homology of $M$, this gives
\[
 H_0(W;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z,\qquad
 \widetilde H_j(W;\mathbb Z)=0\quad(j\ge0).
\]
A simply connected acyclic CW complex is contractible. Indeed any first
nonzero higher homotopy group would, by Hurewicz, give nonzero homology;
if there is none, Whitehead applies to its map to a point. Smooth compact
manifolds have CW homotopy type, so this applies to $W$; see \href{https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch4.pdf}{[E2]},
Section 4.1. If the stated compact-boundary assertion holds, $W\cong D^4$.
The remaining boundary gluing of two standard balls gives $S^4$ by
Cerf's extension theorem. For an orientation-reversing gluing, compose
with a standard reflection extending over a ball and then use the
orientation-preserving theorem.

Conversely, cap such a $W$ by a standard ball to obtain
$M=W\cup_{S^3}D^4$. Van Kampen makes $M$ simply connected and
Mayer--Vietoris gives the integral homology of $S^4$. Hurewicz gives
$\pi_2(M)=\pi_3(M)=0$ and $\pi_4(M)\cong H_4(M)\cong\mathbb Z$.
A map $S^4\to M$ representing a generator is a homology equivalence,
and the simply connected homology form of Whitehead makes it a homotopy
equivalence. If the original conjecture holds, $M\cong S^4$. The
capping ball maps to a smooth embedded standard ball in $S^4$;
Cerf--Palais moves it to a hemisphere. Its closed complement is a
standard $D^4$, and hence so is $W$.\hfill$\square$

The boundary condition cannot be replaced by ``homology sphere'' in
this argument. An acyclic manifold can have a quite different boundary;
without an actual boundary diffeomorphism to $S^3$, the capping step
does not even have the asserted input. Nor is a diffeomorphism of an
open interior by itself the boundary-compatible compact statement
proved equivalent above.

\paragraph{Attempt A: what a cancellation certificate must contain.}
A smooth homotopy sphere admits a finite handle description. Removing
a small ball leaves a compact handlebody, but this does not justify
assuming that every such description has only indices zero, one and
two. Elimination of the three-handles is not an input supplied by
simple connectivity or homology alone.

When there is a description of $W$ with one zero-handle, $r$ one-handles,
and $r$ two-handles and no higher handles, its cellular chain complex
has the form
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z^r
      \xrightarrow{A}\mathbb Z^r
      \xrightarrow{0}\mathbb Z\longrightarrow0.
\]
Rows of $A$, up to the transpose convention, are exponent sums of the
attaching words in the one-handle generators. If $W$ is contractible,
$A$ is unimodular. Integer row and column operations can turn it into
the identity; corresponding handle slides change the algebraic
intersection data. This observation alone does not give the geometric
position required to cancel handles.

The cancellation theorem requires the attaching sphere of the higher
handle and the belt sphere of the lower handle to meet transversely
in exactly one point, with their actual attaching data; \href{https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/surgery-notes.pdf}{[E3]}, Lemma 3.8.
An algebraic intersection number one could instead be the signed sum
$1+1-1$ of three intersections. A matrix entry does not certify that
the extra intersections have been removed by permitted isotopies.
Likewise, altering a word or an integer framing without recording its
geometric realization is not a handle move.

A sufficient proof certificate is therefore a finite list of ambient
isotopies of the framed attaching data, handle slides, introductions of
standard cancelling pairs, and geometric cancellations, ending with a
single zero-handle for $W$. Every step must be legal on the current
boundary and account for the remaining handles. Reversing the resulting
diffeomorphisms gives $W\cong D^4$ and Lemma 22.1 gives $M\cong S^4$.
This proves the conditional implication. No theorem ensuring such a
list for every candidate is supplied here. Failure of a bounded search
for such a list is also not an invariant of the manifold.

\paragraph{An exact test of the homology-only shortcut.}
Consider the balanced group presentation
\begin{equation}\label{cont22:presentation}
 P=\langle s,t\mid s^3t^{-5},\ (st)^2s^{-3}\rangle.
\end{equation}
Its exponent-sum matrix is
\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}3&-5\\-1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det A=1.
\]
The associated presentation complex, with one vertex, two edges and two
two-cells, is consequently acyclic: its $H_1$ is the cokernel of this
invertible matrix and its $H_2$ is the kernel. Yet its fundamental group
is nontrivial. In permutations of five letters, let
\[
 s=(1\ 2\ 3),\qquad t=(1\ 3\ 4\ 2\ 5),
\]
and compose right to left. Then
$s^3=t^5=1$ and $st=(2\ 5)(3\ 4)$, so $(st)^2=1$.
Both relators map to the identity, whereas $s$ does not. This defines
a nontrivial finite image of the presented group.

Thus even a balanced presentation with unimodular matrix cannot certify
simple connectivity. The example is not offered as a homotopy four-sphere,
and no boundary-$S^3$ claim is made for an associated handlebody. It
rejects only the proposed inference from the chain calculation to
contractibility. For an actual candidate whose fundamental group has
already been proved trivial, the further geometric-cancellation problem
still remains. A perfect group example does not prove that any particular
simply connected candidate is exotic.

\paragraph{Attempt B: turn cocores into a potential disproof certificate.}
Suppose a candidate $W$ has been independently certified contractible,
has an explicit boundary identification $\partial W\cong S^3$, and has
a handle decomposition using only indices zero, one and two. A
two-handle $D^2\times D^2$ contains a cocore disk $\{0\}\times D^2$.
Its boundary is a circle in the final boundary. Cocores of different
two-handles give disjoint properly embedded disks.

Choose some $k\ge1$ of these disks and join their boundary circles by
$k-1$ disjoint oriented bands in the boundary, arranged in a tree.
Push band interiors slightly into a collar of $\partial W$, smoothing
the joins to the disks. This gives an embedded connected orientable
surface in $W$. The tree condition joins different components at each
step, leaving one boundary component, and its Euler characteristic is
\[
 \chi=k-(k-1)=1.
\]
Hence the surface is a disk. Under the boundary identification, its
boundary is an explicit knot $K\subset S^3$ which is smoothly slice
\emph{in $W$}.

Let $s(K)$ denote Rasmussen's knot invariant, normalized so that the
unknot has value zero. The established slice-genus inequality \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0402131}{[E4]},
Theorem 1, is
\begin{equation}\label{cont22:slice}
 |s(K)|\le2g_4(K),
\end{equation}
where $g_4$ is the minimum genus of a smooth connected orientable surface
in the \emph{standard} $D^4$ with boundary $K$.

\textbf{Proposition 22.2.} If the preceding construction produces a knot
with a certified value $s(K)\ne0$, then $W\not\cong D^4$, and capping
$W$ gives a counterexample to smooth four-dimensional Poincar\'e.

\emph{Proof.} If $W\cong D^4$, transfer the constructed disk to $D^4$.
Its boundary identification may differ from the prescribed one by a
diffeomorphism of $S^3$. Cerf's extension theorem, with a reflection
if necessary, extends that difference over $D^4$ and restores the
prescribed knot. Thus $g_4(K)=0$, contradicting
\eqref{cont22:slice}. The cap is a homotopy sphere by Lemma 22.1, and
would force $W$ standard if it were standard.\hfill$\square$

This is the established type of test in \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.5177}{[E1]}, Fact 2.1, written out to
show its dependencies. It is not a new counterexample. No candidate
with all the required properties and nonzero $s$ is produced here.
In particular, simply finding a nonslice knot and declaring it to be
a cocore band sum in a homotopy ball would assume the key construction.

\paragraph{Stress tests for the knot route.}
The input disk must be embedded, not merely an immersed disk with
double points. A disk with self-intersections does not give $g_4=0$
after being transferred to a standard ball. The boundary identification
must track the actual knot, not just its homology class: every knot in
$S^3$ has trivial class in $H_1(S^3)$, which supplies no sliceness
information. The band construction explicitly keeps both properties.

The tree condition on the bands also matters. An additional band can
change the number of boundary components or the genus; Euler
characteristic must be recomputed before claiming a disk. If the
constructed surface has genus $g>0$, the same reasoning supplies an
obstruction only when $|s(K)|>2g$. A nonzero value smaller than that
threshold would not suffice.

Conversely $s(K)=0$ is compatible with both slice and nonslice knots;
\eqref{cont22:slice} has no converse in this argument. Zero values on
a finite collection of band sums do not prove $W$ standard. A failed
cancellation search and failed invariant search can therefore coexist
without resolving the candidate in either direction.

\paragraph{Verification, next steps, and outcome.}
The accompanying finite check verifies the determinant and the two
permutation relators in \eqref{cont22:presentation}, using explicit
permutation composition. It does not certify any four-dimensional
diagram. No knot-homology computation or candidate sphere is claimed
to have been verified. The compact-boundary reduction retains the
smooth extension and isotopy theorems as named external inputs.

\textbf{UNRESOLVED.} The strongest conclusions are the compact-boundary

\section*{\texorpdfstring{Smooth 4-Dimensional Poincaré Conjecture}{Smooth 4-Dimensional Poincaré Conjecture}}\label{18}

\subsection{Definitions and mathematical statement}
A closed manifold is compact without boundary. A smooth homotopy $4$-sphere is a smooth closed $4$-manifold $M$ for which there exist continuous maps $M\leftrightarrows S^4$ whose compositions are homotopic to the identities. The conjecture is
\[
 M\simeq S^4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad M\cong_{\rm diff} S^4.
\]
A diffeomorphism must be smooth with smooth inverse. A homeomorphism alone does not settle this smooth-category question.
\par\smallskip\textit{Formulation and concept references:} \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.10938}{[S1]}.

\subsection{Short English statement}
Is every smooth four-dimensional space with the homotopy type of a sphere smoothly the standard sphere?

\subsection{Research attempt}
This unresolved attempt by GPT-6 Astra Ultra was prepared on 27 September
2026, using explicit reductions, source checks, and adversarial verification.

\paragraph{Scope, checked inputs, and two routes.}
The target is a diffeomorphism, not a homeomorphism, for every smooth
closed homotopy four-sphere. This attempt pursues a proof route through
geometric handle cancellation and a disproof route through a compact
contractible manifold with boundary $S^3$. It derives precise sufficient
certificates for each route and tests what information would be lost by
replacing geometry with matrices or a finite group computation.

Gerig \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.10938}{[S1]}, Theorems 1.2 and 1.3, records two inputs used below: an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $S^3$ extends across $D^4$
(Cerf), and equi-oriented embedded closed four-balls in a connected
four-manifold are ambient isotopic (Cerf--Palais). His invariant result
is not a classification of all smooth homotopy spheres. The source
repository \href{https://github.com/toffee-desuwa/smooth4pc-t73-lean/blob/main/docs/INDEPENDENT_REVIEW.md}{[S2]}, under its review boundary, explicitly leaves geometric
interfaces as hypotheses of its formalized implication. No external Lean
code was executed and no counterexample is accepted here on that basis.

The handle and knot strategies have substantial precedents, notably
Freedman--Gompf--Morrison--Walker \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.5177}{[E1]}. What follows is a written derivation
and adversarial check of these routes, without a novelty claim.

\paragraph{Lemma 22.1: an equivalent compact-boundary problem.}
The smooth four-dimensional Poincar\'e conjecture is equivalent to:
every smooth compact contractible four-manifold $W$ with
$\partial W\cong S^3$ is diffeomorphic to $D^4$.

\emph{Proof.} First let $M$ be a homotopy four-sphere, choose a smooth
embedded closed ball $B$, and put $W=M\setminus\operatorname{int}B$.
Van Kampen, applied using boundary collars, gives
$\pi_1(M)\cong\pi_1(W)$ because $B$ and $S^3$ are simply connected.
Thus $W$ is simply connected. Excision identifies
$H_*(M,W;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_*(D^4,S^3;\mathbb Z)$. In the long exact
sequence, the map $H_4(M)\to H_4(M,W)$ is an isomorphism: it sends the
oriented fundamental class to the local relative fundamental class.
Together with the homology of $M$, this gives
\[
 H_0(W;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z,\qquad
 \widetilde H_j(W;\mathbb Z)=0\quad(j\ge0).
\]
A simply connected acyclic CW complex is contractible. Indeed any first
nonzero higher homotopy group would, by Hurewicz, give nonzero homology;
if there is none, Whitehead applies to its map to a point. Smooth compact
manifolds have CW homotopy type, so this applies to $W$; see \href{https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch4.pdf}{[E2]},
Section 4.1. If the stated compact-boundary assertion holds, $W\cong D^4$.
The remaining boundary gluing of two standard balls gives $S^4$ by
Cerf's extension theorem. For an orientation-reversing gluing, compose
with a standard reflection extending over a ball and then use the
orientation-preserving theorem.

Conversely, cap such a $W$ by a standard ball to obtain
$M=W\cup_{S^3}D^4$. Van Kampen makes $M$ simply connected and
Mayer--Vietoris gives the integral homology of $S^4$. Hurewicz gives
$\pi_2(M)=\pi_3(M)=0$ and $\pi_4(M)\cong H_4(M)\cong\mathbb Z$.
A map $S^4\to M$ representing a generator is a homology equivalence,
and the simply connected homology form of Whitehead makes it a homotopy
equivalence. If the original conjecture holds, $M\cong S^4$. The
capping ball maps to a smooth embedded standard ball in $S^4$;
Cerf--Palais moves it to a hemisphere. Its closed complement is a
standard $D^4$, and hence so is $W$.\hfill$\square$

The boundary condition cannot be replaced by ``homology sphere'' in
this argument. An acyclic manifold can have a quite different boundary;
without an actual boundary diffeomorphism to $S^3$, the capping step
does not even have the asserted input. Nor is a diffeomorphism of an
open interior by itself the boundary-compatible compact statement
proved equivalent above.

\paragraph{Attempt A: what a cancellation certificate must contain.}
A smooth homotopy sphere admits a finite handle description. Removing
a small ball leaves a compact handlebody, but this does not justify
assuming that every such description has only indices zero, one and
two. Elimination of the three-handles is not an input supplied by
simple connectivity or homology alone.

When there is a description of $W$ with one zero-handle, $r$ one-handles,
and $r$ two-handles and no higher handles, its cellular chain complex
has the form
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z^r
      \xrightarrow{A}\mathbb Z^r
      \xrightarrow{0}\mathbb Z\longrightarrow0.
\]
Rows of $A$, up to the transpose convention, are exponent sums of the
attaching words in the one-handle generators. If $W$ is contractible,
$A$ is unimodular. Integer row and column operations can turn it into
the identity; corresponding handle slides change the algebraic
intersection data. This observation alone does not give the geometric
position required to cancel handles.

The cancellation theorem requires the attaching sphere of the higher
handle and the belt sphere of the lower handle to meet transversely
in exactly one point, with their actual attaching data; \href{https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/surgery-notes.pdf}{[E3]}, Lemma 3.8.
An algebraic intersection number one could instead be the signed sum
$1+1-1$ of three intersections. A matrix entry does not certify that
the extra intersections have been removed by permitted isotopies.
Likewise, altering a word or an integer framing without recording its
geometric realization is not a handle move.

A sufficient proof certificate is therefore a finite list of ambient
isotopies of the framed attaching data, handle slides, introductions of
standard cancelling pairs, and geometric cancellations, ending with a
single zero-handle for $W$. Every step must be legal on the current
boundary and account for the remaining handles. Reversing the resulting
diffeomorphisms gives $W\cong D^4$ and Lemma 22.1 gives $M\cong S^4$.
This proves the conditional implication. No theorem ensuring such a
list for every candidate is supplied here. Failure of a bounded search
for such a list is also not an invariant of the manifold.

\paragraph{An exact test of the homology-only shortcut.}
Consider the balanced group presentation
\begin{equation}\label{cont22:presentation}
 P=\langle s,t\mid s^3t^{-5},\ (st)^2s^{-3}\rangle.
\end{equation}
Its exponent-sum matrix is
\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}3&-5\\-1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det A=1.
\]
The associated presentation complex, with one vertex, two edges and two
two-cells, is consequently acyclic: its $H_1$ is the cokernel of this
invertible matrix and its $H_2$ is the kernel. Yet its fundamental group
is nontrivial. In permutations of five letters, let
\[
 s=(1\ 2\ 3),\qquad t=(1\ 3\ 4\ 2\ 5),
\]
and compose right to left. Then
$s^3=t^5=1$ and $st=(2\ 5)(3\ 4)$, so $(st)^2=1$.
Both relators map to the identity, whereas $s$ does not. This defines
a nontrivial finite image of the presented group.

Thus even a balanced presentation with unimodular matrix cannot certify
simple connectivity. The example is not offered as a homotopy four-sphere,
and no boundary-$S^3$ claim is made for an associated handlebody. It
rejects only the proposed inference from the chain calculation to
contractibility. For an actual candidate whose fundamental group has
already been proved trivial, the further geometric-cancellation problem
still remains. A perfect group example does not prove that any particular
simply connected candidate is exotic.

\paragraph{Attempt B: turn cocores into a potential disproof certificate.}
Suppose a candidate $W$ has been independently certified contractible,
has an explicit boundary identification $\partial W\cong S^3$, and has
a handle decomposition using only indices zero, one and two. A
two-handle $D^2\times D^2$ contains a cocore disk $\{0\}\times D^2$.
Its boundary is a circle in the final boundary. Cocores of different
two-handles give disjoint properly embedded disks.

Choose some $k\ge1$ of these disks and join their boundary circles by
$k-1$ disjoint oriented bands in the boundary, arranged in a tree.
Push band interiors slightly into a collar of $\partial W$, smoothing
the joins to the disks. This gives an embedded connected orientable
surface in $W$. The tree condition joins different components at each
step, leaving one boundary component, and its Euler characteristic is
\[
 \chi=k-(k-1)=1.
\]
Hence the surface is a disk. Under the boundary identification, its
boundary is an explicit knot $K\subset S^3$ which is smoothly slice
\emph{in $W$}.

Let $s(K)$ denote Rasmussen's knot invariant, normalized so that the
unknot has value zero. The established slice-genus inequality \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0402131}{[E4]},
Theorem 1, is
\begin{equation}\label{cont22:slice}
 |s(K)|\le2g_4(K),
\end{equation}
where $g_4$ is the minimum genus of a smooth connected orientable surface
in the \emph{standard} $D^4$ with boundary $K$.

\textbf{Proposition 22.2.} If the preceding construction produces a knot
with a certified value $s(K)\ne0$, then $W\not\cong D^4$, and capping
$W$ gives a counterexample to smooth four-dimensional Poincar\'e.

\emph{Proof.} If $W\cong D^4$, transfer the constructed disk to $D^4$.
Its boundary identification may differ from the prescribed one by a
diffeomorphism of $S^3$. Cerf's extension theorem, with a reflection
if necessary, extends that difference over $D^4$ and restores the
prescribed knot. Thus $g_4(K)=0$, contradicting
\eqref{cont22:slice}. The cap is a homotopy sphere by Lemma 22.1, and
would force $W$ standard if it were standard.\hfill$\square$

This is the established type of test in \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.5177}{[E1]}, Fact 2.1, written out to
show its dependencies. It is not a new counterexample. No candidate
with all the required properties and nonzero $s$ is produced here.
In particular, simply finding a nonslice knot and declaring it to be
a cocore band sum in a homotopy ball would assume the key construction.

\paragraph{Stress tests for the knot route.}
The input disk must be embedded, not merely an immersed disk with
double points. A disk with self-intersections does not give $g_4=0$
after being transferred to a standard ball. The boundary identification
must track the actual knot, not just its homology class: every knot in
$S^3$ has trivial class in $H_1(S^3)$, which supplies no sliceness
information. The band construction explicitly keeps both properties.

The tree condition on the bands also matters. An additional band can
change the number of boundary components or the genus; Euler
characteristic must be recomputed before claiming a disk. If the
constructed surface has genus $g>0$, the same reasoning supplies an
obstruction only when $|s(K)|>2g$. A nonzero value smaller than that
threshold would not suffice.

Conversely $s(K)=0$ is compatible with both slice and nonslice knots;
\eqref{cont22:slice} has no converse in this argument. Zero values on
a finite collection of band sums do not prove $W$ standard. A failed
cancellation search and failed invariant search can therefore coexist
without resolving the candidate in either direction.

\paragraph{Verification, next steps, and outcome.}
The accompanying finite check verifies the determinant and the two
permutation relators in \eqref{cont22:presentation}, using explicit
permutation composition. It does not certify any four-dimensional
diagram. No knot-homology computation or candidate sphere is claimed
to have been verified. The compact-boundary reduction retains the
smooth extension and isotopy theorems as named external inputs.

\textbf{UNRESOLVED.} The strongest conclusions are the compact-boundary
equivalence, an exact obstruction to a homology-only certificate, and
a fully specified conditional knot certificate. The proof route stops
at geometric simplification of an arbitrary candidate; the disproof
route stops at producing a certified homotopy ball and embedded knot
disk with a nonzero standard-ball obstruction. Concrete next work is
to track framed handle moves on an actual diagram, verify its boundary
as $S^3$, and compute a suitable knot invariant with reproducible input
and grading conventions. Neither a matrix normal form nor a conditional
formal implication alone completes those tasks.
